schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch pair the psalm with the twentieth (prayer answered by thanksgiving), report the Targum/Talmud Messianic reading and Rashi's demurral, and hold the psalm treats David whose cause is figuratively Christ's; Ellicott renders 'the king is exulting in thy might.'

Calvin: a public thanksgiving for the king's prosperity, the Spirit's design to direct the faithful to Christ, 'the end and perfection of this kingdom'; Gill weighs the 'strength' as Jehovah's own or as communicated to Christ as man for redemption.

Henry: David's joy is in God's strength and salvation, not his armies, all with an eye to Christ whose triumphs David's shadowed; Spurgeon lifts it to Jesus the King, proclaimed even on the cross, who as man found his strength in Jehovah.
Augustine reads title and line directly of Christ — in Thy strength 'whereby the Word was made flesh, the Man Christ Jesus shall rejoice.'

Clarke surveys the occasion (Sennacherib, Hezekiah's added years, or most likely David's conquest of Rabbah whose crown he took), owning that many refer the whole to the Messiah — the Targum's 'melech Meshicha.'

debates.question: Is the 'king' David (with Christ as antitype) or directly the Messiah — and what is the occasion?

sides.position: David literally, his cause figuratively Christ's — a thanksgiving for a royal victory (likely Rabbah), with Christ as the end/antitype
the psalm read directly and wholly of Christ the King

outliers.note: Report Rashi's remark that the Messianic interpretation ought to be given up 'for the sake of the Christians,' and caution that even Christian exposition should not press it rigidly.

themes: the king shall joy in thy strength
joy in God's salvation not in armies

schools.summary: Gill hears the prayer of the preceding psalm (Ps. 20:4) answered: whatever Christ's heart desired or his lips requested has been given him.

Ellicott: 'request' is a rare word (root 'to be poor/in want'), the 'not' emphatic, and the prayer for length of life (v.4) suggests it was uttered in sickness, though the psalm's triumph connects it with a victory; Keil and Delitzsch keep the verse as the thanksgiving answering the paired psalm's petition.
Clarke refers the line back to the prayers offered in the twentieth psalm.

outliers.note: From the rare word 'request' and the prayer for life in v.4 suggests the petition was uttered in sickness, while owning the psalm's triumphant tone points rather to a victory — declining to force the occasion.

themes: thou hast given him his heart's desire

schools.summary: Clarke fixes 'prevent' from praevenio, to go before (the collect 'Prevent us, O Lord'; Henry V's 'God before'), rendering 'thou shalt go before him'; Wesley: crowned with manifold blessings, more and sooner than expected.

Ellicott glosses 'prevent' as 'comest to meet him,' and doubts the crown is Rabbah's — perhaps a coronation (Ewald: a birthday), probably only a symbol of victory, the garland maidens offered a returning monarch.

Gill reads spiritual blessings, 'prevented' disclosing their freeness (given before asked), earliness (laid up in Christ from the foundation of the world), and order (first to Christ, then to his people in him).

debates.question: What is the 'crown of pure gold'?

sides.position: the literal captured crown of the king of Rabbah, set on David's head (2 Sam. 12:30)
probably only a symbol of victory and rejoicing — a festal garland, not the spoil of a stormed city

themes: grace that runs ahead of asking

schools.summary: Gill takes the asked-for life two ways — Christ as man receiving resurrection, and life given him for his people, spiritual and eternal, to bestow on all the Father gave him.

Clarke reports but sets aside the Hezekiah reading, taking it of the Messiah of whom David was type; Wesley allows the long life and reign but finds it 'more eminently fulfilled in Christ,' who asked to be saved from death (Heb. 5:7) and received everlasting life.

Keil and Delitzsch read the help of God turning to the king's honour; Ellicott holds 'for ever and ever' merely indefinite length, a courtly salutation (1 Kings 1:31), and warns the eternal Messianic kingdom 'is not to be forced on the passage.'

debates.question: Does 'length of days for ever and ever' reach to the eternal reign of the Messiah, or name only an indefinitely long earthly life?

sides.position: the deathless, eternal reign fulfilled in Christ
merely a term for indefinite length — the Messianic kingdom not to be forced on it

themes: length of days for ever and ever

schools.summary: Gill refers the glory to the King Messiah, great in the Lord's salvation of him (raised, exalted, crowned) or in the salvation of his people wrought by him, the glory rebounding on the Deliverer.

Clarke: the glory 'had its greatness from God's salvation,' no true nobility but of the soul from grace; Wesley reads 'glory' as fame and renown, from the deliverances wrought 'both for him and by him.'
Keil and Delitzsch note the verb of 'honour and majesty' is the word for divine investiture and endowment (Ps. 89:20) — a robe God lays on his anointed.

Henry: the glory 'far transcending that of all the neighbouring princes,' but honour and majesty are laid on him 'as a burden which he must bear, as a charge which he must account for' — carried through to Christ, who received honour and glory from the Father (2 Pet. 1:17; John 17:5) and bears the charge of universal government.

themes: his glory is great in thy salvation
honour and majesty laid upon him
honour as a charge to account for

schools.summary: Ellicott: 'most blessed' is literally 'blessings,' a plural of fulness like Ps. 1:1, and prefers 'in thy presence' to 'with thy countenance' (Ps. 16:11); Keil and Delitzsch mark the verse as the hinge where the psalm's second half begins and the address turns toward the king, and compare the word to Abram, Gen. 12:2 — a possessor of blessing himself and a medium of blessing to others — and read joy 'with' God's countenance as intimate fellowship.

Gill reads 'thou hast set him to be blessings for ever' of the Mediator — not as God but as man, appointed to be redemption, righteousness, sanctification, wisdom, and strength to his people, all irreversible.

Clarke makes the Messiah the source of all blessings for time and eternity, exceeding glad for the joy set before him at God's right hand; Wesley glosses the gladness as God smiling upon him by grace and favour.

Henry: God has made him 'a universal blessing to the world, in whom the families of the earth are, and shall be blessed'; the prophecy has risen to what is peculiar to Christ, since none besides is blessed for ever, much less a blessing for ever.

themes: thou hast made him most blessed for ever
glad with thy countenance / in thy presence
the hinge to the psalm's second half

schools.summary: Gill takes the king for the Messiah (Targum), whose trust reached through his sufferings as man — for support, help, deliverance, and to be heard for himself and his people.
Clarke hears the conqueror's disclaimer — 'not by my skill or valour but by faith in the arm of Jehovah' — and refers 'shall not be moved' to David's prototype, whose throne remains for ever.

Henry makes the king's joy and trust the ground of his people's, unmoved through the mercy of the Most High and not his own merit; Spurgeon presses it to Christ's mastery of the shield of faith, eternal mercy securing the mediatorial throne — the same yesterday, today, and for ever.

themes: the king trusteth in the LORD
the mercy of the Most High

schools.summary: Ellicott marks the psalm turning 'in prophetic strain' from Jehovah to the king, so 'thine hand' is the king's; Keil and Delitzsch ascribe the effect to the king's personal appearing (2 Sam. 17:11), recalling David's decision of Rabbah's fall (2 Sam. 12:26).
Clarke: 'thy uncontrollable power shall find out all thine enemies, wheresoever hidden' — God knows the secret sinner.

Gill musters the enemies of Christ the King — the Jews, the Gentiles, persecuting Rome, the man of sin, nominal professors, the devil and his angels — all to be found out by an omniscient and omnipotent hand.

themes: thine hand shall find out all thine enemies
the address turns to the king

schools.summary: Ellicott finds the figure obscure as it stands and mends it to 'put them into a fiery oven,' drawn from a smelter's furnace not Sodom (Mal. 3:3); 'time of thine anger' is 'of thy face,' the dread majesty here ascribed to the king before the poet refers it to Jehovah 'in his nostril.'
Gill weighs the allusions (David's brick-kiln at Rabbah, or Sodom), allows 'put them into a fiery oven' ('as' for 'into'), and reads wicked men as dry stubble, fuel for the furnace of God's wrath.
Clarke: 'by thy wrath they shall be burnt up,' one class of sinners made to consume another; Wesley: 'like wood, which, when it is cast in, is quickly consumed.'

debates.question: Does the text read 'make them AS a fiery oven,' and whence is the figure drawn?

sides.position: keep the received 'as a fiery oven' — the enemies made to resemble the furnace
a slight change gives 'put them INTO a fiery oven' — a smelter's furnace (Ellicott) rather than Sodom or the brick-kiln

schools.summary: Gill reads 'fruit' of the offspring of the wicked, the fruit of the womb, one with the 'seed' — the sentence falling on the succession, not a generation only.

Ellicott glosses 'fruit' more fully as 'fruit of the womb' (Ps. 127:3; Ps. 132:11, where the fruit of the body is the pledge of a throne's continuance); Keil and Delitzsch set the verse in the closing strophe as the merited recoil of the enemies' own design upon their seed.
Clarke: 'even their posterity shall be cut off, and their memorial shall perish'; Wesley: God takes away 'both root and branch, the parents and all that wicked race.'

themes: the reverse of the covenant with the king

schools.summary: Gill traces all evil, in thought or deed, as ultimately against the Lord; every sin a hostility against God, his Anointed, or his people, the very intention evil and punishable though it never ripen into act.

Clarke finds mercy in the limit — sinners cannot do all in their power, much less all they wish; Wesley: the evil is against God 'not directly, but by consequence,' aimed at David his anointed and at his people, whose injuries God takes as his own.

Ellicott renders it a concession — 'though they have intended evil against thee, have plotted mischief, they have no power at all' — the design real but still-born. Keil and Delitzsch trace the construction to Ps. 27:10 and 119:83 and, with Hitzig, explain the idiom from Ps. 55:4 and 2 Sam. 15:14 — to incline evil down upon a man is to poise it over him so that it may fall in upon him — rejecting the 'spreading of a net' explanation as a phrase not actually found.

themes: evil poised overhead but never dropped

schools.summary: Gill ranges the sense — flee and hide to no purpose, or 'turn behind thy back' (God regarding them no more), or the Targum's 'shoulder,' set apart together for destruction. He presses the separation through history: Christians brought out of Jerusalem before its destruction, the saints called out of Babylon before her fall, the wicked set at Christ's left hand at the last.

Ellicott fixes the literal 'thou shalt put them shoulder' (Vulgate pones eos dorsum), weighs Ewald's 'strike them back,' and compares giving an enemy's neck (Ps. 18:40); Keil and Delitzsch hear the song gather and soar into its closing distich, arrows on the string.
Clarke: God strikes the mightiest army with panic even in victory, so the lame take the prey, making them fly 'as if a volley of arrows had been discharged in their faces.'

themes: thou shalt make them turn their back
panic in the moment of victory

schools.summary: Gill reads the plea for God to exert his strength and be magnified, fulfilled by stages — at Jerusalem's fall, at Babylon's overthrow, and at the last day's everlasting destruction of the wicked.

Clarke presses the paradox — 'Exalt thyself, O Lord; thy creatures cannot exalt thee' — God giving victory while his people stand still, and turns 'praise thy power' into a rule that each celebrates the attribute God showed him most.

Ellicott notes the song turns again to Jehovah, rendering 'we will both with song and lyre celebrate thy power'; Keil and Delitzsch hear the whole close soar into the cry 'Be Thou exalted,' a plea for God's supernal and judicial sovereignty.

themes: be thou exalted in thine own strength
victory while the people stand still
